n: On a sabbath, Jesus walked through grain fields, and his disciples picked heads of grain, rubbed off the husks in their hands, and ate. Luke’s detail shows exactly what the Pharisees called “work.”

f.g: An unclear phrase in the Greek; many manuscripts simply say “a sabbath.”

n: Some Pharisees challenged them: why are you doing what is forbidden on the sabbath? To them, plucking was reaping and rubbing was threshing.
Jesus answered: haven’t you read what David did when he and his men were hungry?
David entered God’s house and ate the consecrated bread meant only for priests, and shared it with his men. Mercy and need can outweigh ritual rules.

f.g: The “bread of the Presence,” twelve loaves placed before the Lord.

n: And he declared that the Son of Man is Lord of the sabbath — he has authority over the day he himself established.
On another sabbath he taught in a synagogue where there was a man whose right hand was withered. Luke the physician notes which hand — the one needed for work.
The scribes and Pharisees watched closely to see if he would heal on the sabbath, looking for grounds to accuse him.
Jesus knew their thoughts and told the man to get up and stand in front of everyone. He did.
Jesus asked them: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good or harm, to save a life or destroy it? Their plotting that very day was itself the real sabbath-breaking.
Looking around at them all, he told the man to stretch out his hand. He did, and it was completely restored.
They were filled with fury and discussed what they could do to Jesus.
Jesus went up into the hills and spent the entire night praying to God. He prepared for an important decision through long prayer.
At daybreak he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, naming them apostles — “ones sent forth.”

f.g: Greek apostolos, a messenger sent with authority.

n: The list: Simon, whom he named Peter, and his brother Andrew; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew.
Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot — possibly once part of a movement opposed to Rome. A former tax collector and a zealot served side by side.

f.g: “The Zealot” — someone zealous for the law, perhaps tied to anti-Roman nationalists.

n: Judas son (or brother) of James, also called Thaddaeus, and Judas Iscariot, who became the traitor.

f.g: The Greek says only “Judas of James,” usually meaning son of James.

n: Coming down, he stood on a level place with many disciples and a huge crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and be healed. Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon is called the “Sermon on the Plain.”

f.g: A level place, perhaps a plateau on the mountainside.

n: Those troubled by evil spirits were also healed.
The whole crowd tried to touch him, because power was going out from him and healing them all.
Looking at his disciples, he said: blessed are you who are poor, for God’s kingdom is yours. Luke’s beatitudes speak directly (“you”) and include real poverty. Matthew adds “in spirit.”
Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh. God will reverse present sorrows.
Blessed are you when people hate you, exclude you, insult you, and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man.

f.w: cast out your name as evil
f.g: Slander your reputation, perhaps expel you from the synagogue.

n: Rejoice and jump for joy then, because your reward in heaven is great — their ancestors treated the prophets the same way.
Luke adds four “woes” that mirror the blessings. Woe to you who are rich — you have already received your comfort.

f.g: An expression of grief and warning — “how sad for you.”
Comfort — they’ve had their reward already.

n: Woe to you who are full now — you will be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now — you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when everyone praises you — that’s how their ancestors treated false prophets. Popularity is not a sign of truth.

f.w: when all men shall speak well of you

n: To those willing to listen: love your enemies and do good to those who hate you. This is the heart of Christian discipleship.
Bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you.
If someone strikes your cheek, offer the other. If someone takes your outer cloak, don’t withhold your tunic. Refuse to retaliate.
Give to everyone who asks, and don’t demand back what someone takes. Generosity over grasping.

f.w: Give to every man that asketh of thee

n: Treat others the way you want them to treat you — the “Golden Rule.”

f.w: as ye would that men should do to you

n: If you only love those who love you, what credit is that? Even sinners do that.

f.g: What credit or favor is that to you?

n: If you only do good to people who do good to you, what credit is that? Sinners do the same.
If you lend only when you expect repayment, what credit is that? Even sinners lend to sinners expecting full repayment.

Love your enemies, do good, and lend without expecting anything back. Your reward will be great, and you’ll be children of the Most High, who is kind even to the ungrateful and wicked. We become like God by loving as he loves.
Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Luke’s version of Matthew’s “be perfect” centers on mercy.
Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven.

f.g: The JST of the parallel adds: judge not unrighteously.

f.w: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven

n: Give, and you will receive — a full measure, pressed down, shaken to settle, and overflowing into your lap. The measure you use will be used for you.

f.g: The fold of a robe above the belt, used like a pocket to carry grain.

n: He gave a comparison: can a blind person guide a blind person? Won’t they both fall into a pit? Choose guides who can truly see.

f.w: Can the blind lead the blind?

n: A student isn’t above the teacher, but a fully trained student will become like the teacher. Disciples become like whom they follow.
Why notice the speck of sawdust in someone else’s eye but ignore the plank in your own? A humorous picture of hypocrisy.

f.g: A large wooden beam or plank.

n: How can you offer to remove your brother’s speck while ignoring your own plank? Hypocrite — first remove your own; then you’ll see clearly to help him. Self-correction comes before correcting others.

f.w: cast out first the beam out of thine own eye

n: A good tree doesn’t produce rotten fruit, and a rotten tree doesn’t produce good fruit.
Each tree is recognized by its fruit. You don’t pick figs from thorns or grapes from brambles. Character shows in actions.

f.w: every tree is known by his own fruit

n: Good people bring good things out of the good stored in their hearts; evil people bring out evil. What fills the heart comes out of the mouth.

f.w: of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh

n: Why call me “Lord, Lord” and not do what I say? Words without obedience are empty.
Jesus describes someone who comes to him, hears his words, and acts on them.
That person is like a builder who dug deep and laid the foundation on rock. When the flood came and the torrent crashed against the house, it couldn’t shake it.

f.w: laid the foundation on a rock

n: But the one who hears and doesn’t act is like someone who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the torrent hit, it collapsed at once, and its ruin was complete.
